output.title: The Cutting of the String
output.prologue: I am Sil, the Moon, the Drowned Lantern, and Aun was my brother. He was the First Flier, and he wanted to know how far the wind went, so he cut the string Mother Hesk had held at the pole. The sky drifted up and away. I went after it along the tide, and I am still going. Come with me. We will fly the sky from the pole to the Unflown, and I will tell you what each lamp remembers.

stops.text: *Kavet* — "the Drop Spindle." Here Mother Hesk sat at the pole, drawing the string out thin and winding it on her whorl so the islands would not drift. I was on the Lamp Road then, low and round, and I saw everything. Aun came up to the pole with his knife in his teeth. He did not look down at the islands. He looked up, and the string gave like a held breath.

*Ketsa* — "the Nanny at the Edge." In the hungry winter the hearths ran low, and the herders brought the goats in past the door-stones one by one. A grey nanny with a torn ear would not come. She stood on the ledge with her feet in the wind, looking up at the place where the string had been. I stopped beside her, because I knew how she felt. A thing left out has to watch the way things went.

*Hasket* — "the Drop Spindle, the second one." When Aun cut the string, Mother Hesk was spinning the new thread that would have held the sky close. The wind took her spindle from her fingers and it fell, and the thread ran out behind it, unfinished. I passed beneath it on my way down the Lamp Road. Hesk looked at her empty hands for a long time. Then she began to count.

*Halveth* — "the Widow's Split-Tail." When a fisher is drowned, his widow flies this kite alone on the first calm day. It has two long tails, and they never pull together. I came down the sky to see her. She had no one to hold the second line, so she tied both tails to her own wrists and let the wind pull them apart. I did not tell her that is how I have flown since Aun.

*Telvar* — "the Lamp Kite." When Aun cut the string and the sky drifted off over the water, the boats on the Upper Sea lost their way in the dark. Those on the rocks could see nothing. So I hung my light low over the shoals, on a kite-string, and told the boats which way was home. It was not enough light for the whole sea, only enough for the ones who were looking.

*Mirske* — "the Tally Kite." When Aun first flew it, he tied a knot in the tail for every winter he had come through alive. By his third spring the tail was heavy with them. I have counted his winters since. I do not know how many he has come through, so I count the winters I have waited instead. It is the only sum I am sure of, and I tie a new knot at every new moon.

*Naveth* — "the Widow's Shawl Sail." Tamun's husband went out to haul the lines in a grey squall, and Tavo the Gale came laughing over the Upper Sea and took his boat. He went aloft as a kite. Tamun wrapped herself in the sail he left on the shore, and she would not take it off. Tavo does not give back what he takes. Tamun is still waiting for the shawl to come home.

*Lamet* — "the Name-Kite." When old Tenu went aloft, his grandchildren sewed his name onto a strip of sailcloth, one knot for each letter. They flew it at midsummer, when the light stays up all night. I flew beside it, for I have lost names too. From them I learned that a name must be knotted, not only spoken, or the wind forgets it. Aun's name takes three knots. I tie them every night.

*Varosk* — "the Ebb Hound." When Aun cut the string he was in a hurry, and he left his hound on the shore below the cliffs. Varosk was grey, and his teeth rang like bells when he shook the wet from his coat. He would not follow the sky. He lay on the wrack and watched the tide go out, the way a hound watches a door. I asked him where his master had gone. He rang his teeth at me.

*Sarra* — "the Cut Kite." She was the best fighting kite on the Leeward shore, with a tail of knotted sailcloth and a bridle nobody could bend. Every spring she cut the lines of the kites that challenged her, and every spring more came. I asked her whether she had seen a man with a knife. She said she had seen only wind, and the wind was not fighting, only going. Then she cut my line too, to see whether I would fall.

*Hanor* — "the Plumb-Line." When Aun cut the string, the sky went up so fast that his sister Sil had to run after it along the tide. I ran. Before he let go, Aun had tied a stone to the last of the cord, so the end would sink and not fly. I still feel the weight of that stone in my hand. It is how I know he meant to come back.

*Varo* — "the Unpaid Crossing." When Aun cut the string, the first things to drift past the last lamp were the drowned, and none of them knew the way. A grey-bearded boatman of the Upper Sea took them over and asked no fare. I went down to the water's edge and asked for passage. He said he had not carried my brother, and he would not say whether he had seen him. He only said that the crossing here is free, and no one pays twice.

*Thavesk* — "the Turned Wake." Aun built a boat of cloth and bone and sailed it south, past the last island, because he wanted to see where the wind stopped. Here the water tilted under him, and his wake turned back on itself like a shuttle going home. I found the wake still turning. I put my hand in it, and it was warm, as a thwart is warm after the rower has stood up. He had been here, and he had not stopped.

*Hunal* — "the Ram in the Surf." He was a ram of the cliffs above the north shore, and he loved one goat more than grass. One spring she ran out along a sea-stack, and Hunal ran after her, out along the narrow rock with the sea white on both sides. It was a foolish run, and nobody who has loved anything has ever said otherwise. The surf has them both now. I keep the place where the rock goes under.

*Kavesk* — "the Cut End." When Aun cut the string, the sky went up but did not come all the way free. A short length of cord stayed knotted to his hand, and it still hangs at the bottom of the Unflown. I found it at last. I took hold of it. It was cold and frayed, and it tugged once, as a line does when there is a fish or a brother on the far end. I have not let go since, and I do not mean to.
